prose:d-2-tanzania-93bef4: Tanzania operates one of the more mature national health management information systems on the African continent, consolidating routine facility reporting across all levels with programme data from areas such as HIV, malaria, immunisation, and maternal and child health. It demonstrates how a large, geographically diverse country can consolidate multiple programme data streams into a coherent national information system, and offers lessons on data-quality governance, subnational capacity building and the management of facility reporting burden.
prose:d-2-uganda-d83254: Uganda's national health management information system, managed by the Ministry of Health, provides aggregate reporting across the public health system and has progressively integrated community health worker reporting, logistics data and surveillance. Uganda has also participated in piloting computable decision logic derived from WHO SMART Guidelines. The example is notable for the integration of community-level data into national aggregates and for early evidence on operationalising internationally developed computable guidance in a national system.
prose:d-2-united-kingdom-england-a7ab86: England governs pharmaceutical decision support centrally — providing interaction checking, allergy alerting and dosage guidance to prescribing systems across primary and hospital care — and operates a national terminology service hosting the SNOMED CT UK Edition and the dictionary of medicines and devices. It demonstrates how centrally governed pharmaceutical knowledge and terminology can be deployed through standardised interfaces to a diverse ecosystem of consuming systems, reducing duplicated maintenance and improving consistency of medication-safety guidance.
prose:d-2-united-states-f02f9f: The United States illustrates centralised knowledge governance with distributed consumption through the CDC immunisation decision-support logic (CDSi), consumed by a diverse ecosystem of immunisation systems and clinical applications [cdc-cdsi], and population-scale syndromic surveillance (BioSense) that draws on clinical data already generated at the point of care [cdc-nssp]. Both illustrate the governance of shared capability across a highly decentralised system with multiple jurisdictional authorities.
prose:d-3-european-union-and-european-ec: The European Surveillance System (TESSy) is a regional platform through which member states submit standardised communicable-disease surveillance data to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control for regional analysis and international reporting [ecdc]. It demonstrates how a supranational authority can operate shared surveillance infrastructure across sovereign jurisdictions with diverse national systems, and offers lessons on cross-border data-sharing governance, indicator standardisation and the management of variation in case definitions within a common framework.
prose:d-3-who-smart-guidelines-pilot-imp: Several countries — including Ethiopia, the Philippines and Uganda — have piloted the deployment of L3 computable decision logic for areas such as antenatal care, HIV and immunisation within national health information systems. These pilots provide early evidence that internationally developed computable guidelines can be operationalised nationally, reducing the time and cost of adapting international clinical guidance for national deployment.
prose:e-40301a: Goal: core health data is captured once and reused reliably across programmes, services, and levels of care.
prose:e-ce763f: What the health system needs to be able to do: the health system needs authoritative, uniquely identified reference data — who people are, who provides care, where, with what products, and under what terms — held once and made available to every application component that needs it, rather than re-collected and reconciled in each. It needs that data to be well governed, current, and trustworthy, so that the systems built upon it can rely on it without duplicating or re-verifying it.
prose:e-d53f92: Unlike the goals that follow, this one has no mapping of its own. It is the foundation the other six draw on. Each of those mappings traces back to the same shared components — the client, health facility, and health workforce registries, the terminology service, the product registry, and the lifelong health record — and the recurrence of those components across goal after goal is the "capture once, use many times" principle made visible. The composition of that foundation, the minimum a country puts in place first, and how it matures over time are set out in the REDDHI framework in Section 2.2; the spreadsheets in this appendix show that foundation being reused, goal by goal.
prose:e-5534a6: Goal: a health system that ensures the right number and skill mix of trained health and care personnel with the right skills are in the right place at the right time to meet population health needs, and a health workforce whose members — across both regulated professions and non-licensed or community cadres — are individually identifiable and verifiable (Sub-goal 2.1), equitably deployed and retained where they are needed (Sub-goal 2.2), paid reliably and on time in compliance with labour rights (Sub-goal 2.3), supported to maintain and extend their competencies across the course of their careers (Sub-goal 2.4), and backed by trustworthy registration and authorisation status that safeguards patient safety, public accountability, and worker privacy (Sub-goal 2.5).
prose:e-f3eb0f: What the health system needs to be able to do: the system needs to know who all of its health and care workers are and what each is qualified and authorised to do — covering statutory licensed practitioners overseen by health practitioner regulators as well as non-regulated cadres, community health workers, multiskilled personnel, provisional registrants, students and trainees, and volunteers authorised through national programme or employer mechanisms where formal licensure or foundational national identity is absent. It must hold an authoritative reference record of workforce identity, occupational and role classification, educational qualifications, and professional registration or authorisation status that clinical, administrative, financing, and regulatory systems can rely on, while explicitly separating verified registration and qualifications from current clinical competence, task-specific authorisation, facility-level clinical privileging, fitness to practise, and authorised scope of practice (which depend on ongoing clinical governance, credential verification, supervision, competence assessment, and regulatory standing). To align with the WHO National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) and the health labour market framework, it needs to distinguish among workers who are licensed to practise, professionally active, and practising, and enable national and subnational planners and policymakers to track active workforce capacity, skill mix, and subnational distribution so that imbalances in the health labour market can be identified and minimised. Rather than inferring staffing adequacy from worker location and facility affiliation alone, the system needs analytical and planning capabilities that combine workforce deployment, contract/full-time equivalent (FTE) capacity, and scope of practice with catchment population need, service demand, workload, facility readiness, and infrastructure data, alongside external statistical and administrative sources of varying digital maturity (such as population censuses, labour force surveys, and national pension or social-security schemes). Finally, it needs to pay workers reliably and uphold labour rights (including salary, leave, pension, accreditation, and continuing professional development) by connecting verified workforce identity and active deployment records with operational HR, contract, attendance, public financial management, payroll, and learning systems — keeping detailed HR administrative actions, extended leaves, pay calculations, and course-level learning records inside those operational systems while enforcing strict compliance with data confidentiality and privacy laws, purpose-limited dataset sharing, worker transparency, and avenues for correction and appeal.
prose:e-b1992f:
How to read the mapping: the spreadsheet and capability summary that follow trace each workforce sub-goal (2.1–2.5) through stakeholder value, business capability, and application service to the shared DPI-H components, foundational-DPI dependencies, and operational workforce-management systems required to realise the goal, noting where shared components are reused across other goals:

  • Shared DPI-H reference components versus operational workforce systems: the mapping centres on three shared DPI-H components — the Health Workforce Registry (a core foundational registry reused across clinical care, surveillance, supply chain, and health financing), the Health Facility Registry, and the Terminology Service — resting on foundational-DPI identity, trust/verifiable credentials, payment rails, data exchange, and single sign-on services. However, these shared registries alone cannot deliver Goal 2 without the operational systems that consume and update them: Human Resources for Health Information Systems (HRHIS) and employer HRIS, civil-service and facility payroll, contract management, public financial management (PFM), time and attendance, shift scheduling, deployment management, professional regulatory council platforms, clinical privileging and supervision tools, pre-service education and accreditation systems, learning-management systems (LMS), and workforce-planning and health labour market modelling applications. In particular, foundational payment DPI provides disbursement rails but does not determine employment validity, salary calculation, attendance, deductions, payment authorisation, or budget availability (which belong to HR, contract, attendance, payroll, and PFM systems); similarly, the Health Workforce Registry holds authoritative qualification and high-level continuing professional development (CPD) compliance references, whereas detailed learning activities, curricula, supervision logs, and competency assessments belong to LMS, education, and accreditation systems.
  • Care-services discovery model and dual national/international terminology governance: linking workforce and service delivery requires more than joining a worker identifier to a facility identifier. The mapping aligns the Health Workforce Registry, Health Facility Registry, and Terminology Service with a full care-services discovery model — such as the IHE Mobile Care Services Discovery (mCSD) profile — capturing the distinct relationships among Organisation (employer, regulator, or provider organisation), Practitioner (regulated or non-regulated worker), PractitionerRole (role, specialty, authorised scope of practice, task-sharing authority, contract/FTE basis, and active period), Location / Facility, and HealthcareService. Because international classifications alone cannot represent country-specific cadres, multiskilled workers, community health work, task sharing, or local scope of practice, the Terminology Service governs national occupation, role, specialty, credential, and scope-of-practice vocabularies separately and maintains structured mappings to international classifications — ISCO-08 (WHO health worker classification framework) for occupations and ISCED (International Standard Classification of Education) for educational qualifications — alongside interoperability with multi-source national data (regulatory registers, censuses, labour force surveys, and pension schemes) to populate NHWA indicators across licensed to practise, professionally active, and practising statuses.
  • Boundary of registry data, privacy compliance, and purpose-limited reuse: the Health Workforce Registry must comply with national data confidentiality, privacy, and data-protection laws. Detailed HR administrative records (such as extended leaves of absence, internal administrative or disciplinary proceedings, performance appraisals, and pay/deduction schedules) are held in employer HRIS and payroll systems; the shared registry records only the resulting high-level operational deployment status and regulator-issued licence/authorisation status. To prevent unnecessary exposure of personal residential addresses, nationality, disciplinary histories, salary details, or employment terms during payroll validation or workforce planning, the architecture enforces purpose-specific datasets and role-based access controls, provides de-identified or aggregated datasets for workforce planning and NHWA reporting, and gives health workers audit transparency into access to their records together with formal mechanisms for correction and appeal.
  • Suggested phased implementation sequence: countries can sequence these capabilities progressively as infrastructure matures: (1) Phase 1 — Governed workforce identity, classification, and registration/authorisation status, establishing unique workforce identifiers across licensed and non-licensed/CHW cadres, governed national role and qualification terminology mapped to ISCO-08 and ISCED, authoritative registration/authorisation status, and privacy, correction, and appeal controls; (2) Phase 2 — Organisational affiliations and mCSD care-services discovery, linking Practitioner, PractitionerRole, Organisation, Facility/Location, and HealthcareService records with NHWA activity statuses (licensed to practise, professionally active, practising) and contract/FTE data; (3) Phase 3 — Workforce planning analytics, LMS/CPD integration, and payroll/HR validation, combining aggregated workforce, facility, service-demand, workload, catchment-population, and external statistical/pension data for shortage mapping, connecting LMS/accreditation systems for CPD compliance, and integrating HRIS, attendance, PFM, and payroll systems for payee validation and NHWA compensation reporting; and (4) Phase 4 — Cross-border and regional credential verification and mobility reporting, enabling bilateral or regional verification of credentials and ethical recruitment monitoring.
prose:e-37b7cf:
[HG2_Health_Workforce_Mapping]

Sub-goal / Mapping row Health-system & worker outcome Shared DPI-H & DPI-F capabilities Operational systems, governance & standards
2.1 High-quality workforce data for planning, deployment and shortage mapping (Right Place / Equitable deployment and distribution) Ensure the right number and skill mix of trained health and care personnel are equitably distributed and retained across subnational areas and levels of care to meet population health needs, tracking NHWA licensed to practise, professionally active, and practising stock and inflows/outflows across the health labour market. Health Workforce Registry, Health Facility Registry, and Terminology Service linked via IHE mCSD care-services discovery patterns (Organisation, Practitioner, PractitionerRole, Location/Facility, HealthcareService); Health Management Information System (aggregated service/workload metrics); foundational geospatial and data-exchange DPI. Operational HRHIS/HRIS, deployment, scheduling, and workforce-planning / health labour market modelling applications combining workforce FTE, contract type, and scope of practice with catchment population need, service demand, workload, and facility infrastructure; interoperability with population censuses, labour force surveys (national statistical offices), and national pension/social-security schemes; purpose-limited de-identified/aggregated planning views.
2.2 Reliable and timely remuneration and compensation analytics (Timely Pay) Pay health and care workers accurately, reliably, and on time in compliance with labour rights, eliminate ghost workers and payroll leakage, and inform reporting on NHWA indicators on expenditure for compensation, entry-level wages and salaries, and pay gaps. Health Workforce Registry (verified workforce identity, active registration/authorisation, and primary/secondary facility affiliation references); Health Facility Registry; foundational digital identity and payment DPI disbursement rails. Operational payroll, HRIS, contract-management, time-and-attendance, payment-authorisation, and public financial management (PFM) systems (which govern employment validity, salary and allowance calculation, deductions, extended leaves, administrative actions, and budget availability outside the shared registry); aggregated payroll feeds for NHWA remuneration and pay-gap indicators.
2.3 Identity, verifiable qualifications, registration, clinical privileging, and cross-border mobility (Proven Skills) Establish governed identity, educational qualifications, and regulatory registration or alternative authorisation for both statutory licensed professionals and non-licensed/community cadres (CHWs, multiskilled workers, provisional staff, trainees, volunteers), separating registration from current clinical competence, task-specific authorisation, facility privileging, fitness to practise, and scope of practice. Health Workforce Registry, Terminology Service (governing national occupation, role, specialty, credential, and scope-of-practice vocabularies mapped to ISCO-08), and foundational identity, trust, and verifiable-credential DPI. Health practitioner regulators (licensing councils/boards), programme/employer authorisation workflows, facility clinical privileging, supervision, and competence-assessment systems; bilateral or regional credential-verification mechanisms where established by law, alongside foreign-trained stock and mobility monitoring aligned with the WHO Global Code of Practice on the International Recruitment of Health Personnel (which establishes ethical recruitment principles, workforce sustainability, and data exchange/reporting rather than mandating a specific digital cross-border verification protocol).
2.4 Continuous competency and career development (Continuous Growth) Support health and care workers to maintain and extend their competencies, specialisations, and scopes of practice across their careers through accredited pre-service education, continuing professional development (CPD), and clinical supervision. Health Workforce Registry (recording authoritative qualification references, specialist credentials, and high-level CPD compliance/licence-renewal status); Terminology Service hosting the ISCED taxonomy (International Standard Classification of Education) for educational qualifications alongside national credential and specialty code sets. Operational learning-management systems (LMS), pre-service education and training-tracking platforms, educational accreditation bodies, and clinical supervision systems (which manage detailed learning activities, course completions, competency assessments, and training records outside the shared registry).
2.5 Safety, accountability, and privacy-preserving workforce data governance (Cross-cutting trust & data protection) Enable patients, facilities, payers, and regulators to trust that a practitioner's registration, licence, or authorisation status is current — preventing payroll fraud and unsafe or uncredentialed care — while protecting worker privacy and labour rights. Health Workforce Registry standards-based query APIs with role- and purpose-based access control, audit logging, and consent/disclosure controls; foundational trust, authentication (SSO), and audit DPI. Compliance with national data confidentiality, privacy, and data-protection laws; purpose-specific datasets (restricting access to residential address, nationality, disciplinary records, salary, and HR admin notes); worker transparency into data access and formal procedures for record correction and appeal.

Normative references informing the Goal 2 mapping: (1) World Health Organization (2023), National Health Workforce Accounts: A Handbook, Second Edition; (2) World Health Organization (2010), Classifying Health Workers: Mapping Occupations to the International Standard Classification (ISCO-08), together with the UNESCO International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED) taxonomy for education and qualifications; (3) World Health Organization (2015), Human Resources for Health Information System: Minimum Data Set for Health Workforce Registry (with updated WHO HRHIS guidance in preparation); and (4) World Health Organization (2010), WHO Global Code of Practice on the International Recruitment of Health Personnel.
prose:e-3d3f79: Goal: care that is informed by a person's full health history, guided by current evidence at the point of care, and coordinated across every provider, setting, and episode a person moves through.
prose:e-2238ff: What the health system needs to be able to do: the system needs to assemble a person's longitudinal record from the many places care is given and present it as a single coherent view, so that each encounter builds on what came before rather than starting afresh. It needs to make current, evidence-based protocols and decision support available to health workers as they make decisions, and to support the safe delegation of clinical tasks across cadres according to scope of practice. And it needs to coordinate care over time — referrals, transitions between settings, shared care plans, and follow-up — while tracking adherence and quality so that gaps and duplication can be seen and corrected.
prose:e-1325e8: How to read the mapping: the spreadsheet that follows traces each capability from the goal through stakeholder value, business capability, and application service to the DPI-H components and foundational-DPI dependencies that support it, and notes where each component is reused by other goals. Despite its breadth, the goal rests very largely on shared infrastructure other goals already require — the client registry to resolve a single patient identity across sources, the health workforce and facility registries to attribute care to verified providers and sites, the terminology service to keep clinical meaning consistent, and the lifelong health record as the shared longitudinal store every provider reads from and writes to. The genuinely new DPI-H component the goal introduces is the Clinical Decision Support Engine, which delivers context-aware, guideline-based recommendations at the point of care and has no direct equivalent in earlier reference architectures. The operational systems that carry out the work — point-of-care clinical applications, care-coordination and referral tools, electronic prescribing, laboratory and imaging systems — consume these shared components rather than being defined by DPI-H.
prose:e-405b00: Goal: every person has a verifiable digital health record that they can access and control, and that authorised providers can rely on across the places they seek care.
prose:e-ec7f55: What the health system needs to be able to do: the system needs to resolve each person to a single, verifiable identity and to assemble their longitudinal record so that it can be reached wherever care is given. It needs to let people see and govern who accesses their information, through consent that can be granted, recorded, and withdrawn. And it needs to assure the authenticity and integrity of records and of the people and institutions that contribute to them, so that a record can be trusted by a provider who did not create it.
prose:e-9cdd54: How to read the mapping: the spreadsheet that follows traces each capability from the goal through stakeholder value, business capability, and application service to the DPI-H components and foundational-DPI dependencies that support it, and notes where each component is reused by other goals. This goal is distinctive in introducing no new DPI-H component of its own: it is the goal the foundational shared-data layer exists to serve, realised through the client registry and the lifelong health record, supported by the workforce and facility registries for accountable, verified contribution and by the terminology service for consistent meaning, and resting on foundational-DPI trust services together with the cross-cutting consent and security properties addressed elsewhere in this guidance. The patient-facing applications through which people view and manage their records consume this foundation rather than being defined by DPI-H.
prose:e-0e6ccd: Goal: safe health products reach the people who need them, when and where they are needed, through a supply chain that is visible end to end and able to adapt when demand shifts.
prose:e-97c216: What the health system needs to be able to do: the system needs to forecast demand and plan supply against budgets and programme priorities, and to see stock levels and product movement from source to point of use. It needs to identify products, locations, suppliers, and individual batches consistently, so that an item can be traced through ordering, storage, transport, and dispensing, and recalled or removed when needs arise. And it needs to connect these flows to the rest of the health system — to facilities, to financing, and to the people who ultimately receive the products.
prose:e-73950f: How to read the mapping: the spreadsheet that follows traces each capability from the goal through stakeholder value, business capability, and application service to the DPI-H components and foundational-DPI dependencies that support it, and notes where each component is reused by other goals. The goal leans on shared infrastructure other goals already require — the health facility registry to locate every point in the network, the terminology service to standardise product and service codes, and the client registry where dispensing is traced to the individual — while the components specific to this domain are two reference registries: a Product Registry that lets products be identified and traced consistently across the network, and a Supplier Registry that records provenance and supplier accountability. The operational systems that run the supply chain — forecasting, order, warehouse, procurement, transport, and dispensing applications, including the tracking of individual batches and serial numbers — consume these shared registries rather than being defined by DPI-H.
prose:e-deab37: The method is illustrated in full for this goal in the worked example in Section 2.4.2.
